newsitem.title: UK: British agency OK's plan to burn mad cow carcasses.
newsitem.headline: British agency OK's plan to burn mad cow carcasses.

text.p: The carcasses of cattle slaughtered in mad cow disease eradication programmes can be burnt in power stations with "negligible" risk to humans, an independent British agency said on Wednesday.

The Environment Agency said test burnings of meat and bone meal from slaughtered cows showed that the risk of it infecting a human with Creutzfeld Jakob Disease (CJD), the human equivalent of mad cow disease, would be as low as one in 30,000 million.
"This is 3,000 times less than the risk of death by lightning," the agency said in a statement.
Under the programme thousands of cattle have to be slaughtered and their carcasses disposed of safely. There are currently about 300,000 tonnes of slaughtered cattle in store awaiting disposal.
The agency, which polices government policy and will present its findings to the government, carried out trials last year at two coal-fired power stations.
The agency's director, David Slater, said: "Our studies show that the risk to both the public and the environment from the waste disposal options related to the cattle cull is negligible."
He said, however, that the agency was not giving blanket approval to all applications to dispose of cattle waste materials in power stations.
"We will only grant approval if we are fully satisfied that all statutory requirements are met," Slater said.

Britain has slaughtered thousands of cattle since it emerged in March last year that humans could become infected with a version of the fatal brain wasting disease Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).

Britain's cattle farmers were devastated when the European Union imposed a global export ban in response to the mad cow scare. Fifteen months later, the government still has no idea when the ban might be lifted.
Earlier this month, the government said it had identified 17 probable and definite cases of the type of CJD that has been linked with mad cow disease.

The Environment Agency said its tests on methods of cattle waste disposal showed that in one year, no individual person would be likely to consume more than a minute fragment -- significantly less than one millionth part -- of the dose of BSE needed to cause infection in humans.
